title: Joshua 1:1–9
context: After the death of Moses, the LORD speaks to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ servant, and commissions him to arise, cross the Jordan with all the people, and enter the land God is giving Israel. The gift is stated in terms already spoken to Moses: every place the sole of Joshua’s foot will tread, with borders from the wilderness and Lebanon to the Euphrates and the great western sea. The LORD promises to be with Joshua as he was with Moses, and that he will not fail or forsake him. Three times Joshua is told to be strong and courageous. That courage is joined to careful observance of the law Moses commanded, to meditation on the book of the law day and night, and to the promise that the LORD his God is with him wherever he goes. Both traditions read the unit as a divine commissioning for the work that follows, grounded in the sworn land promise and in God’s faithful presence, not in Joshua’s self-confidence. The repeated charge to be strong and courageous, and the promise of the land, are shared ground.

verses.text: Now after the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD spoke to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses’ servant, saying,
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrative begins “after the death of Moses the servant of the LORD”. The LORD himself then speaks to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ servant, so the succession is not left to human appointment alone.

Arminian readers hear a real word spoken to a named servant who must now take up the work. Grace initiates, and Joshua is actually addressed and will have to respond.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise stress that the book opens with the LORD’s speech. Joshua’s authority rests on that word, and Moses’ title, “the servant of the LORD,” names a finished stewardship, not a vacancy God cannot fill.

Both traditions take the verse as divine commissioning at a moment of loss. Joshua’s leadership begins with God’s own initiative, shared ground for the chapter that follows.

verses.text: “Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go across this Jordan, you and all these people, to the land which I am giving to them, even to the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Moses my servant is dead.” He then commands Joshua to arise, go across this Jordan with all the people, and enter “the land which I am giving to them, even to the children of Israel.”

Arminian readers hear a genuine command to arise and go. The land is God’s gift, and the people must actually cross in obedient response to the giver.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the present gift: the land is what the LORD is giving. Moses’ death does not cancel the promise. The command to cross is the way that already-spoken gift will be taken up.

Both traditions read the land as God’s gift and the crossing as a commanded act, not as Israel’s self-made claim on Canaan.

verses.text: I have given you every place that the sole of your foot will tread on, as I told Moses.
verses.arminianNotes:
“I have given you every place that the sole of your foot will tread on, as I told Moses.” The gift is spoken as already granted, and it will be walked out in the days ahead, in the terms already given to Moses.

Arminian readers hear promise and walking held together. The people must actually tread the ground, and they do so under a word already spoken.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the settled grant in “I have given”. The foot’s treading does not create the gift; it enters what God has already given, matching what he had told Moses.

Both traditions take the verse as the fulfillment of that earlier word to Moses, not as a new or lesser promise.

verses.text: From the wilderness and this Lebanon even to the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites, and to the great sea toward the going down of the sun, shall be your border.
verses.arminianNotes:
The borders run from the wilderness and Lebanon to the great river, the Euphrates, include all the land of the Hittites, and reach “the great sea toward the going down of the sun,” which shall be their border. The description is geographic and generous, in line with the land’s earlier bounds.

Arminian readers hear a real grant with real borders. The people are being told where the promised inheritance extends, not given a merely poetic image.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the borders as the LORD’s own description of the gift, reaching as far as he said, not as far as Joshua might invent.

How fully Israel later occupied this whole extent is a historical question readers in both traditions weigh; the verse itself states the promised border, and both take that statement as God’s word.

verses.text: No man will be able to stand before you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not fail you nor forsake you.
verses.arminianNotes:
No man will be able to stand before Joshua all the days of his life. As the LORD was with Moses, so he will be with Joshua: “I will not fail you nor forsake you.”

Arminian readers hear a personal promise that meets a real need for courage. Joshua can rely on this word as he obeys; the presence is pledged, not presumed from his office alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the comparison with Moses and the double promise of presence and of not failing or forsaking. The same God who upheld Moses now binds himself to Joshua.

Both traditions take the verse as a covenant pledge of God’s faithful presence, the true ground of Joshua’s security in the work ahead.

verses.text: “Be strong and courageous; for you shall cause this people to inherit the land which I swore to their fathers to give them.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Be strong and courageous”, for Joshua shall cause this people to inherit the land the LORD swore to their fathers to give them. The first of the chapter’s three charges ties courage to the sworn inheritance, not to self-trust.

Arminian readers hear a genuine exhortation. Joshua must be strong, and he can be, because the oath to the fathers stands and the work is God’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the courage is commanded because the inheritance is already sworn. Joshua will cause the people to inherit what God promised the fathers; the oath, not Joshua’s nerve, secures the gift.

Both traditions read “Be strong and courageous” as shared ground: a real charge, grounded in the LORD’s oath to the fathers.

verses.text: Only be strong and very courageous. Be careful to observe to do according to all the law which Moses my servant commanded you. Don’t turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.
verses.arminianNotes:
He must be strong and very courageous, and careful “to observe to do according to all the law which Moses my servant commanded you.” He is not to turn to the right hand or to the left, that he may have good success wherever he goes.

Arminian readers hear success bound to a real, careful obedience. The path is not indifferent; Joshua is responsible to keep the whole law entrusted through Moses.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise join courage to obedience. The law Moses commanded remains the rule of the new leader’s way, and “good success” is promised in that path, not apart from it.

Both traditions take the verse as a call to unswerving fidelity to the written law, not to military improvisation alone.

verses.text: This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, that you may observe to do according to all that is written in it; for then you shall make your way prosperous, and then you shall have good success.
verses.arminianNotes:
“This book of the law shall not depart from your mouth,” and Joshua is to meditate on it day and night and to observe to do all that is written in it; then he will make his way prosperous and have good success.

Arminian readers hear a practiced, responsible life under Scripture. Meditation and obedience are real acts Joshua must keep up, and prosperity is held out along that path.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the book itself is to fill Joshua’s mouth and his days. Success is attached to what is written, so the leader is ruled by the LORD’s law, not by private insight.

Both traditions take this as a classic charge to constant meditation on Scripture and to doing what it says.

verses.text: Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Haven’t I commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Don’t be afraid. Don’t be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go.”

Arminian readers hear the command itself as a ground of courage. Joshua is not left to invent strength; he is told not to fear because God’s presence goes with him, and he must take that word to heart.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hear the same question as a reminder that the charge comes from God. Fear and dismay are answered not by Joshua’s temperament but by the promise that the LORD his God is with him wherever he goes.

Both traditions take the repeated call to be strong and courageous as grounded in God’s command and presence, shared ground for the crossing that follows.
